title: Baking Moon Dirt Into Breathable Air
kidSummary: Moon dirt isn't like garden soil—it is crushed gray rock full of trapped oxygen! With enough heat and electricity, astronauts can bake oxygen straight out of lunar dirt.
scienceDetail: NASA's ISRU (In-Situ Resource Utilization) experiments show lunar regolith is ~40–45% oxygen by mass, bound in silicate and oxide minerals like ilmenite. Extracting it locally cuts rocket launch weight.

title: Why Astronauts Stack Moon Dirt on Their Roof
kidSummary: Earth has a giant invisible magnetic bubble and thick air that block Sun storms. The Moon has neither! Stacking thick walls of moon dirt acts like armor against space radiation.
scienceDetail: NASA DONKI tracks Coronal Mass Ejections and Solar Proton Events (>10 MeV). Without a magnetosphere, lunar surface crews need thick regolith shielding or storm shelters to keep doses safe.
nasaSourceName: NASA Space Weather Database (DONKI) & Radiation Physics

title: Why Batteries Matter When the Sun Sets
kidSummary: A single night on the Moon lasts about two whole Earth weeks, and temperatures drop colder than any freezer! Solar panels make zero power in the dark, so crews must charge batteries early.
scienceDetail: One lunar synodic day lasts ~29.5 Earth days (~14.7 days of sunlight and ~14.7 days of darkness), with shadowed temperatures plunging below -130°C to -246°C at Shackleton Crater. In Silica Station, the dark period is simplified to 5 rounds (Rounds 5–9) for classroom play.
nasaSourceName: NASA Artemis Lunar South Pole Environment

title: Moon Dust Sticks Like Static Cling
kidSummary: Lunar dust is sharp like tiny glass shards and carries static electricity, so it sticks to spacesuits and solar panels—blocking sunlight until astronauts clean them.
scienceDetail: Apollo missions found that electrostatically charged lunar dust abrades seals, coats radiator surfaces, and reduces photovoltaic array efficiency unless actively mitigated.
nasaSourceName: NASA Lunar Dust Mitigation & Apollo Lessons

title: Frozen Water Hiding in Dark Craters
kidSummary: Deep craters near the Moon's South Pole never see sunlight. They hold ancient frozen ice that rovers can mine and split into drinking water and air!
scienceDetail: NASA's LCROSS and LRO missions confirmed water ice deposits inside Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs) near Shackleton Crater—the prime target for Artemis base camps.
nasaSourceName: NASA LRO & LCROSS Water Ice Discovery

title: Why Moon Astronauts Never Skip Exercise
kidSummary: On the Moon you weigh six times less than on Earth! That sounds fun, but without daily workouts, astronauts' bones and muscles shrink fast.
scienceDetail: NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and ISS crew studies show microgravity and partial gravity cause bone mineral loss and muscle atrophy unless countered by daily resistive exercise.

title: Measuring Real Astronaut Radiation in Space
kidSummary: Invisible cosmic rays hit astronauts faster than on Earth! Radiation sensors aboard the Space Station measure exact dose rates every minute so engineers know how much armor crews need.
scienceDetail: NASA OSDR's RadLab database combines real absorbed dose rate (µGy/hour) readings from ISS instruments like DosTel1 and DosTel2. Dose rates spike sharply when passing high-radiation zones, proving why thick lunar regolith shielding is critical.
nasaSourceName: NASA OSDR RadLab Radiation Dosimetry Portal

title: Growing Fresh Food on the Moon & in Remote Communities
kidSummary: Rockets can't bring fresh salad every week! Astronauts grow leafy greens, berries, and veggies inside energy-saving Moon greenhouses—and the same tech helps Northern towns on Earth grow food all winter.
scienceDetail: The Canadian Space Agency (CSA) & Deep Space Food Challenge pioneer Controlled Environment Agriculture (CEA): closed-loop hydroponic systems that reuse water, conserve electricity, boost astronaut nutrition, and serve remote Northern communities.
nasaSourceName: CSA · Food Production on the Moon & in Remote Areas

title: Space STEM Activities for Kids Ages 7–12
kidSummary: Want to try real space experiments at school or home? The Canadian Space Agency shares free hands-on games, coding challenges, and moon-farming activities for young explorers.
scienceDetail: CSA's Space Resources for STEM and Youth Organizations provides bilingual activities designed for classrooms, libraries, camps, and clubs to connect space exploration with nutrition, robotics, and sustainability on Earth.
nasaSourceName: CSA · Space Resources for STEM & Youth
